Ada Research 
Purpose and Aims                
With the increasing role of algorithms in our daily lives, there is a growing need to understand the binary operations of code and how it filters our world. Even if ‌digital resolution increases, the world seems to gravitate to the stereotypical. This is especially prevalent in ‌content in 3D libraries, apps, and platforms where there is a lack of diversity[1]. The potential of algorithms is vast but the usage is predictable. Based on fixed taxonomies the reinforcement algorithm tries to keep us using the apps. The artistic research project Ada Research seeks to challenge this predictability by exploring alternative visions and expanding the understanding of 3D worlds.


Ada Research is a virtual reality (VR) world and a meta-quest into 3D computer vision. The name originates from Ada Lovelace, the world's first programmer, who wrote about the relationship between computers and generative art in 1842[2]. The project seeks to explore ‌the digital margins and simulate patterns to help negotiate how digital algorithms create invisible fences. The project aims to enhance our understanding of how algorithms, as digital tools, shape our bodies, creativity, and subjectivity.


By creating an immersive virtual reality world that guides the player through a landscape of algorithms, the research aims to provide new insights into the hidden complexity of these mathematical constructs. This exploration describes and visualizes a world with increasingly complex control structures. With four ambitious work packages, the research starts with basic algorithmic concepts[3] like noise and vectors and eventually progresses to topics such as generative reality and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Each package creates new game items, fantastical spaces, and game logic based on the algorithms researched. Over time the VR world gets populated with strange realities that the player is guided through. The game extends into anamorphic and exploratory spaces reflecting and negotiating the margins of the ongoing research. 


​​Central to the investigation is how fluid queer[4] potential is coded. The world-building procedure seeks to show how complex algorithms, for instance, drag celebration and fluid simulation, inherently challenge us to find new ways to see the world. However, in the apps, applications, and platforms the binary stereotypes such as heteronormative gender beliefs and other cultural boundaries have a strong pull and content seems to gravitate towards the normative. The more algorithms increase in complexity, the more tools, platforms, and apps seem to take shortcuts. By recognizing algorithms as performative elements that modify different passages, the queer perspective can offer a critical lens through which to explore the power dynamics and social implications of algorithms.


The project draws inspiration from the history of art, particularly the utopian interplay between abstract and surrealist movements. It extends that relation by looking at the role visual thinking plays in mathematics and seeks in the margins to find hidden queer forms. Building on the margins of algorithms, the project explores the concept of entropy to hopefully find a queer ontology at its heart. 


The project is a collaboration between Konstfack, The Royal Institute of Technology Stockholm and Design Academy Eindhoven, and several individual artists. I will lead the project and produce new insights through artistic methods and exploration. To identify the margins the project manages a complex pipeline between art, science, and future industry. KTH will push the insights with deepening knowledge about systems and mathematics alongside DAE who also provides insights into the applied complexity of VR installations. This collaborative approach brings diverse perspectives and expertise to create a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding. The expected outcomes include the VR world, exhibited installations, a book, and a game wiki documenting the game and explaining the algorithms of simulations and geometry. The body of work is a fantastical world and a playground of joy, beauty, subversion, and exploration. An updated and expanded version of Paul Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook (1953) in drag, in VR, a one-of-a-kind open-source resource to help researchers, artists, and students understand and think with algorithms to learn from, imagine with, and build on. 

  

Can we put Paul Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook (1953) in Virtual Drag?
State of the arts
The emergence of modernism challenged hegemonic power with utopian ideas that were often related to rethinking realism, manifesting in abstract and surreal art long before digitalization. Recent development has reopened a quest beyond the real. Driven by algorithms, increasingly realistic simulations challenge the borderland between the real and synthetic, fake and original[5]. DeepFakes[6] are fake videos, images, and audio voice cloning that are difficult to distinguish from the original. Artificial intelligence improves the mimicking of human creativity, and new large language models like ChatGPT write code and produce scientific writing​​. This algorithmic blur of the real opens up both threats and opportunities. On the one hand, manipulation and fake news have poisoned the political realm in the last decade - reinforcing bias and misinformation on social platforms. On the other hand, the space beyond the real has queer and surreal potential. The procedural algorithms and virtual cameras can morph into new spatialities, metaphors, and queer cyborg subjectivity. Contemporary art that explores algorithms has a unique possibility to reflect and transform new realities. Here I want to mention four fields that make up contested possibilities where I situate the research. 
1 Machine Learning
The release of the first convolutional neural network (CNN) AlexNet (2012) marked a significant advancement in machine learning (ML), with numerous subsequent contributions to the field. One notable is Leon A. Gatys' paper, A Neural Algorithm of Artistic Style[7], (2015) Implemented in Google's Deep Dream[8], the algorithm demonstrates the surreal and queer potential as any content can take an alternative form. Machine Learning (ML) algorithms gained recognition as strange portraits made by the French collective Obvious using GauGAN were sold at Christie's auction house for $432,500. A Study of Invisible Images (2017) by Trevor Pagleno offers insights into how ML algorithms perceive the world and how it shapes our understanding of reality. Ian Cheng's BOB (2018-2019) explores contingency and unpredictability in an AI simulation. In recent years, Deep Learning text-to-image platforms like Stable Diffusion (2022)  and Midjourny (2022), have opened up a new way to make images using text prompts, models for Music like in Riffusion (2022) and 3D objects like Goggles DreamFusion (2022). The models make content creation more democratized but also destabilize human creativity. 
2 Critical Technology - exploring the hidden
AI and ML models image generators propagate gender and race stereotypes. Here one possible scenario is endless gravitation towards more of the same. Joy Buolamwinis's work The Coded Gaze (2016) raises awareness about the need for more diverse data sets in AI technologies and opens up the discussion of bias and representation in computer models. Other artists shed light on new surveillance protocols and explore the logic behind hidden power structures. In Loophole for all (2013) and Derivatives (2019), Paolo Cirio uses hacking strategies to explore the power behind the selective use of datasets. Adam Harvey's CV Dazzle (2010) shows how to avoid facial recognition with beautiful camouflage. Hito Steyerl's How Not to Be Seen: A Fucking Didactic Educational. MOV File (2021) examines the politics of visibility. Harun Farocki analyzes the inherent power and violence of technology. "Eye/Machine" (2001) is a trilogy of films that investigates the role of weaponization of images, and as Farocki phrased it, “[T]hese are images that do not represent an object, but rather are part of an operation.”[9] Recent social technology has substantial weight in defining our subjectivity, and software steers our cognitive patterns more than ever. The artistic research into computer vision and new digital realities is essential for the project because they lay the foundation for alternative queer becoming. 
3 Algorithmically inspired art 
Computer vision informs the expansion of algorithmic art in various fields, including painting, sculpture, and large-scale installations. Some contemporary examples are ‍Petra Cortright and Ken Okiishi's screen-based paintings and the blobby nature of David McLeod's 3D worlds. Rachel Rossin's expanded paintings, the anamorphs of Zach Lieberman, and the hallucinatory world of Refik Anadol. How Mariko Mori places herself in a sci-fi future and how Lynn Hershman Leeson's works explore the intersection of mind and machine. Sougwen Cheang’s, fluidø (2017) explores augmented robotics. These are all works of growth and point to queer morphologies of the future. 
4 Exploratory 3D 
The immersive environment of VR allows for the creation of interactive environments that challenge viewers' narratives of history, space, and time. Examples of artists who have utilized VR to explore these themes include Jacolby Satterwhite, whose 3D animations delve into queer identity and the body, and Sondra Perry, who has used VR technology to create installation and immersive environments that explore themes of race and identity.


The steady stream of new 3D content creates residue from works as a base material in Jon Rafman and Ed Atkins's work - assemblages situated in the endless archive. Ongoing research in computer vision and the development of new algorithms, for instance, queer fluid simulation and soft bodies are repackaged in an alternative surreal form in Albert Omoss’s Undercurrents (2016) and Nikita Diakur’s Ugly (2017). 


The dimensional and queer desire has sister fronts in other disciplines. In architecture, notably Zaha Hadid’s Heydar Aliyev Center (2003). And in computer games, the dimensional drive challenges the limitations of three-dimensional space, for instance, Fez (2012), Miegakure (ongoing). An adjacent dimension drive is found in a game pop culture on youtube, bugs, glitches, Machinima, and the tech Demo Scene. The dimensional desire feeds on open-source tools and platforms such as Processing, more accessible game engines like Unity 3D and Unreal, other 3D software like Blender with all its addons, and 3D sculpting tools like Tilt Brush. These platforms lower the threshold for digital creativity and create new intricate pipelines. Central is also the ecosystem of software studies and tutorials like Daniel Shiffman, youtube channel The Coding Train, his book Nature of Code (2012), and the coding adventures of Sebastian Lague. As the line between tools and creativity blurs, Faster GPU:s, Ninites, world creators, AI objects, and disturbed render networks are a few examples of the way we create content in the future.
Significance and scientific novelty
Alternative Visions undercutting the Binary Code
Ada Research aims to visualize alternatives to streamlined stereotypes, surfaces, and images. The project examines the boundaries of digital worlds and platforms by pushing ‌content, that is driven by norms and cliches, to its technological margins into unseen forms. As our digital literacy increases, we start to see the otherwise hidden operating forces of algorithms all over; Perlin Noise can explain the procedural and blobby world of art, architecture, and computer game landscapes, vectors explain painting and financial markets, and the math behind entropy explains contemporary sculpture and cryptography. 


By working in a unique, VR-integrated, and exploratory way the project is able to present vision algorithms in a new way in order to articulate and widen the spectrum of art and what we see. The project probe for ‌the queer within the technical, algorithmic, and mathematical ontological object itself. 
Transdisciplinary collaboration and new research tools 
In a field where multiskilled exploration is essential, the project uses a collaborative approach, involving workshops with the Royal Institute of Technology Stockholm, Design Academy Eindhoven, and several individual artists. These explorations open up new intersections between art, science, and technology, with great potential for generating new insights and perspectives into the digital world. Through computer game development the research shows we can use tools of play to advance our understanding. The world-building process can foster hands-on design, layering, exploration, implication, articulation, and documentation in the same VR space in a unique way.
Preliminary and previous results 
I spent 25 years at the forefront of using computer games as artistic tools and exploring the performative potential of internet protocols. 


Between 2012 and 2014, I conducted a research project on the potential of hackerspaces and participatory networks, funded by the Swedish Research Council, that has informed the current project. The earlier research now moves into the VR world to explore vision algorithms.


The current project has a one-year feasibility study funded by Konstfack. In the study, I created a work called "Radical Inside" (2021), which explores the hidden surreal and queer potential of visual 3D platforms and algorithms. See the peer-reviewed article in the Nordic Journal for Artistic Research[10] about the work. The hackerspace and mixed reality lab I have built at Konstfack provide a foundation for the current project. The lab has already allowed me to start testing some of the ideas and work proposed in their project, and a grant would enable a deep dive into this field for further analysis. With the one-year course in programming that I hold for professional artists at Konstfack, I likewise documented and explored relevant platforms and algorithms. Central to the practical and theoretical frameworks is also a course I developed at Konstfack called Queer 3D-worlds[11]. Here, I use the same technical pipeline as in the proposed research project. 


I have already scratched the surface of this research project when I created the first prototype of the VR game called "Ada Research" during the summer of 2022. The game focuses on visual desire and includes a landscape with meandering patterns created by Kristina Torsson and the fashion company Mah-Jong. As players progress through the game, they visit science labs that explore the history and current development of various algorithms, and I can explore the inside of 3D models. The algorithms become more generative as the game progresses and ultimately ask players to consider the possibility of merging with the VR world by examining the paradoxes, such as infinity and entropy.


  

Detail, VR installation, Ada Research, Bilds, Vamlingbo, Gotland,  2022.
Project description 
Theory 
The goal of the project is to understand how algorithms affect the way digital tools and systems work and how they control our bodies and creativity. To help with this exploration, an investigation into complexity and entropy is central.
Queer Embodiment 
In the age of AI, digital materiality is algorithmic and performative. To embody this, I find great inspiration in the theoretical work and life of cryptographer and mathematician Alan Turing, as I find that different areas of inquiry intermingle in his work: entropy, questions of AI, mathematical paradoxes, spatial desire, generative queer morphology, topology and geometry, and queer joy and death. 


* Turing proposed the Turing machine, which laid the theoretical foundation for modern computers in 1936. The Turing machine was an answer to the "Entscheidungsproblem," or decision problem, which questions the fundamental law of mathematics, and furthered the undecidable foundation of mathematics.
* Based on the mathematics of entropy, Turing is known for cracking the encrypted messages of the Nazi Enigma in 1942, which helped the Allies win World War II.
* In 1950, he formulated the Turing test, a test of a machine's ability to exhibit intelligent behavior indistinguishable from humans. Turing's concept of the "B-type unorganized machine," which he described in 1948, was a precursor to modern neural networks.
* In 1952, Turing posed and solved the leopards' spots problem using mathematical morphology.
* The same year, the UK convicted Turing of gross indecency due to his homosexuality, which was still illegal. He chose chemical castration over imprisonment, but the treatment made him impotent and depressed, and he took his own life in 1954.
Entropy
The key to finding cross-connections between the points above is entropy, which simply put is a measure of disorder or uncertainty in a system, and a fundamental concept in thermodynamics and information theory. In information theory, difference requires more complex encoding than sameness. As we step towards more entropy, noise - information, difference, and diversity increase. 


Hito Steyerl's concept of the poor image explores how images can be heavily compressed and disseminated quickly. Poor images are often of lower quality and may not accurately represent the original content, but they are still influential due to the reduction of speed of communication.
Roger Penrose, a theoretical physicist, has suggested that the universe protects us from the inherent unpredictability of singularities by hiding them behind event horizons or margins. From Turing's cryptic letter "Messages from the Unseen World”[12] Penrose argues that human thought is too advanced to be algorithmic and that consciousness must have a quantum physics basis that can escape entropy. The world must be abstracted and the process can risk suppressing elements that do not fit. 


In AI there is a trade-off between overfitting and underfitting. If a model is overfitting, it may be too complex and have a high entropy cost, while if it is under-fitted, it does not capture the problem at hand. The prediction of computer models has a complexity cost that goes to infinity and incompatibility. Behind the world of digital discreteness, there is a theoretical black hole. On the margins of a queer quest, the project seeks new comprehension. 
Misframing
Even if digital resolution/complexity increases, procedural algorithms are further developed and hybridization is possible, the world seems to gravitate to the stereotypical. John Law writes about Othering (2003), everything that is not independent, prior, definite, and singular, which refers to excluding or marginalizing certain groups or individuals based on perceived differences. Othering can lead to the suppression of diversity and the reinforcement of monocultures, which have low entropy and resilience. Judith Butler's theories of Precarious Life (2001) point to how some life is less valued, and Nancy Frasers writes about misframing (2008) - certain issues or problems are framed in a way that excludes or marginalizes certain groups.
Algorithmic misframing
As technology strives to become natural and invisible, it often abstracts and simplifies complex processes behind interfaces, which can lead to the algorithmic enclosure of our social systems of knowledge. This enclosure is an expression of power that threatens the core values of democracy. Evgeny Morozov describes it as "invisible barbed wire" (2013), and Shoshana Zuboff as the "Big Other" (2015). In Algorithms of oppression (2018), Safiya Umoja Noble examines how algorithms and search engines can reinforce and amplify existing inequalities and biases. Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence (2021), Kate Crawford writes about the hidden costs of AI and how AI damages the environment, fuels inequality, and shifts toward undemocratic governance. In a society controlled by technology, transferring control to simplified interfaces obscures reality. 
Queer forms, grammar, and morphology
The research draws from Donna Haraway's ideas on "making kin, not population" (2018) and her cyberfeminist thoughts. Haraway writes: "The cyborg is a creature in a post-gender world; it has no truck with bisexuality, pre-oedipal symbiosis, unalienated labor, or other seductions to organic wholeness through a final appropriation of all powers of the parts into a higher unity." [13] (1986) She argues that the cyborg and other margin-creatures and critters offer a way to move beyond traditional dichotomies and create new ways of understanding ourselves and our place in the world. The queer studies of Sara Ahmed, Queer Phenomenology (2006), and the affinity of Happy Objects (2010) are vital to understanding queer objects and their orientation and disorientation. John Allan describes ‌stretched, folded, or twisted space as a way to transcend power in Topology of Power (2016). In A Thousand Plateaus (1980), Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari write about rhizome, the body without organs, the war machine, and the plane of immanence - all topological metaphors pointing to open-ended processes and systems that are fluid, dynamic, and non-hierarchical. We can relate these arguments to the 3D world and modeling, topology, and entropy - the trade-off between several polygons (polycount) and the possibility of deforming a body smoothly.


Hacker ethics
The project tries to implement a visual world of care and repair that aligns with the principles of the open knowledge ecology of free software (Stallman 1983). Ivan Illich's ideas on the social materiality of technology in Tools for Conviviality (1973) ‌highlight the transparency and repairability in promoting collaboration beyond the dominance of experts. Paulo Freire's concept of reflection and action directed at transforming structures in Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968) is also relevant to this research as a way to avoid the instrumentalization of technology. The research explores the potential of technology to empower individuals to be more autonomous drawing from the concept of commoning (Caffentzis & Federici, 2014). Feminist and queer perspectives can show ways to create a new grammar that avoids the capture of stereotypes and shows creative strategies toward a reparative morphology in societies where surveillance, algorithmic control, and xenophobia are growing. In Feminism and the Politics of Commons (2011), Silvia Federici reflects on how a new commons is evolving from the informatization and cognitivization of production. Federici describes how networked technology can enable new collective political subjects; however, the capitalist spirit seems to suffocate it. 
Methods
The project uses many different methods:

* Using VR technology to create an immersive environment for exploring and interacting with digital materials and landscapes. 
* Using game development tools and processes to create interactive experiences that enable documentation, articulation, implication, and presentation in the same VR space
* Using transdisciplinary collaboration involves artists, designers, and researchers from various fields to bring together different perspectives and expertise. 
* Using ‌a hands-on exploration of the virtual environment to develop a new language and widen the spectrum of art and what we see. 
* Using artistic exploration to examine the cultural boundaries of digital worlds and platforms by pushing content driven by norms and cliches to unconventional margins and unseen forms
* Using intersections between queer theory and generative art and game development to explore the queer within the technical, algorithmic, and mathematical ontological object itself.
* Using documentation of the process and results of the research in various forms, including the VR world, a book, installations, and a game wiki.
Time plan and implementation
The research consists of five work packages to be ‌distributed over the research period. All packages could build on the previous packages to create a truly queer game experience. It takes half a year to complete one iteration at a 50% activity grade estimated from experience and ongoing studies. VR game development is a complex process, from research to implementation and testing. This estimate means the project delivers two iterations per year and four major packages or releases during the first two years. In the project the last year is dedicated to optimizing the final release and making the final publication about the project. Here is the negotiable outline of the content of the four first packages.



* 1. Basic Elements. Implementing the foundational algorithms that are essential for creating generative art, such as Randomness and Fibonacci. It could also include more concrete algorithms such as Perlin noise, Voronoi diagrams, sine curves and resonance frequencies, Sound experiments, and Particle systems to create basic elements of the game environment or objects ​​and build a solid foundation for more complex algorithmic exploration. 
* 2. Advanced Elements. Implementing more complex algorithms that enable the creation of more sophisticated forms, such as Fractal subdivision, Flow fields, Fourier transforms, L-systems, and Cellular automata. This package also explores the algorithmic topology of desire and the creation of queer meshes and textures for instance in soft body simulation deformable objects, such as cloth, liquids, rubber, and ​​other simulation algorithms.
* 3. Pattern and World Building. Implementing algorithms that enable the creation of unique and dynamic patterns and game environments, such as Reaction-diffusion systems, Graph Theory, Procedural generation, Neural networks, Shading algorithms, and Evolutionary algorithms. How do we navigate an auto-generated world?
* 4. Advanced Techniques. Implementing cutting-edge algorithms, such as Swarm intelligence and Chaos theory and further exploring algorithmic life and AI. In this package, we also deal with non-euclidean spaces.

Each package will consist of an exploration phase, a workshop-test phase, and a documentation-release phase. As project leader, I will use Agile methods to manage communication and collaboration, receive feedback, identify any issues, and remain adaptable to change throughout each work package.

  

1. Exploration phase
Building on the earlier documentation, feasibility study, and the pipeline from earlier VR works I enter the experimental prototyping phase. The method I use for my research begins with an exploration and implementation of the specific algorithms. I experiment with algorithmic systems, learning about their inner workings and pushing them to their limits to understand their capabilities and limitations. I utilize programming experiences and artistic methods I have developed over the years to uncover hidden paradoxes. I keep a coding diary where I document my process and articulate the grammar. Along with notes, I also save versions of my work at each stage and involve synthesizing existing literature on the topics. 
2. Workshop-test phases
After the exploration, collaboration, feedback, and co-creation with Design Academy Eindhoven and from KTH, the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm will start. Benoit Baudry professor at KTH will help guide the understanding of applying the work pack to computer vision. Baudry will also help create, test, and ensure a reliable complex pipeline between and openness of the software systems. Ian Biscoe professor at Design Academy Eindhoven will help to layer possibilities in the VR world and think about spatial configuration central to the decimation of complexity in the work. I host game testing workshops where the ground is discussed on the theoretical and technical challenges with each partner.


After package two, the research expanded the workshop group. Some renowned artists I have contacted and am happy to be involved, artists Rosa Menkman, Evan Roth, Anna Uddenberg, and Geraldine Juarez. The reference groups will help guide the aim of the research in exploring how the VR work can handle the tension between different dualities, such as order and disorder, function and dysfunction, accessibility and complexity, explicit and implicit qualities, and visible and invisible logic. 
3. Documentation-release phase
Data management is at the heart of the research project. GitHub works as an iterative publication tool (with version control to create, store, and update) to ensure transparency, openness, reproducibility, and long-term data management for each stage in each work iteration of the project. The props, algorithms, and labs of the game are documented in a fandom-like game wiki. Documentation is an integral part of the project. 
Public display and The final publication 
Years two and three also create exhibitions in galleries or institutions, nationally and internationally. To name two possible partners, I have been in discussions with Marina Schiptjenko (gallerist, Stockholm) and Acute Art (London). There will be at least four large exhibitions. Last year, I intensified the documentation and dissemination of the project. Finally, an extensive publication collects documentation of all the environments and props with deep explanations and critical reflections. The expected outcomes include the VR world, exhibited installations, a book, and a game wiki. The book documents the grammar and gives an overview of the complete project. The body of work becomes a new tool and resource to help researchers, artists, and students ‌understand and think with queer algorithms. This work will be a one-of-a-kind open-source resource to learn from, imagine with, and build on.
Equipment
The project requires high-end VR headsets, Oculus Rift, and high-performance computers to create and experience the virtual reality world. Access to Konstfack's equipment and facilities, including the hackerspace and mixed reality lab, will be available for the project. 


The need for research infrastructure, Project organization, and International and national collaboration does not require further explanation.

documents.text:
The Void Tower is a building under construction. Its floors are incomplete, its elevator shafts open, and its architecture offers no guarantee of safe passage. You may descend by following the stairs, crossing a bridge, or falling through an opening in the floor. There are machines, abandoned materials, experiments, and inhabitants whose purposes are not immediately apparent. The building is not a ruin, although it carries the residues of previous activities. Nor is it an unfinished version of some ideal architectural plan. Its incompleteness is becoming a condition of its existence.

I began Ada Research with a related problem. In the original research proposal from 2023, I wrote that even as digital resolution increases, the world seems to gravitate toward the stereotypical. Computer graphics had become capable of producing increasingly complex and realistic environments, yet the commercial libraries, interfaces, and platforms through which these environments were constructed continued to reproduce remarkably narrow ideas of bodies, beauty, identity, and space. The technical potential was vast, but its realization appeared increasingly predictable.

A beautiful grotesque need not be a monster that has been repaired. It can be a body released from the obligation to become anatomically correct, visually seamless, or recognizable as human.

Its beauty may emerge through transformation, excess, choreography, and the pleasure of inhabiting an impossible form.

The capacity to generate an extraordinary number of alternatives is not the same as the capacity to determine which alternatives matter.

The next frame is not given.

documents.text:
QFEP means Queer Free Energy Principle. Ada proposes a critical, relational extension of the questions surrounding prediction and persistence: whose conditions of living does a model support, what differences can it register, and who can contest its terms?

Q asks that a model remain revisable while what it leaves out retains capacities to live, act and change those terms. Omitting a difference from a representation and destroying its conditions of existence are different acts. A more accurate prediction does not, on its own, settle whether its use is desirable. Neither greater intelligence nor a larger entropy value guarantees care.

Self-Q returns the question to the maker. What we build also trains what we notice and imagine next. The project's three questions ask what capacities a structure makes possible, what it forecloses, and what inhabits the part it cannot see. These are questions for judgment, not another score to maximise.

More open branches are not automatically better. Shelter, refusal and protective boundaries can sustain possibilities; arbitrary disturbance can destroy them. The research commitment is to attend to those consequences and keep the authority of the model open to challenge. The fan's count cannot make that decision for us.

What must this system change so that difference can do more than fit?

# Ada Research — Full Handover: Knowledge, Critical Attention and Composition for `final.md`

**Date:** 14 October 2026  
**Status:** Editorial and technical strategy, implementation proposal, **not** applied to the repository  
**Repository:** `palletorsson/AdaResearch`  
**Branch audited:** `palm-scanner-door-entry`  
**Commit inspected:** `0870d9b04ff048df916c0a47312e67347237d502`  
**Audience:** Astra / local coding agent, book/editorial collaborators, AI-assisted research workers  
**Priority:** Add the missing critical-knowledge composition process for `final.md` without replacing the existing tutorial, museum, experiment, or task systems.

## Executive directive

**Preserve two distinct but reciprocal text practices.**

- `tutorial.md` establishes operational capacity: a learner can build, predict, compare, modify and reconstruct an explicitly supplied mechanism. Its technical ghost student and eventual independent learner test reveal missing prerequisites, errors and hidden dependencies.
- `final.md` establishes a situated, critical, associative encounter: it follows the material and mathematical operation, seeks its **edge, leak, technical bias and attachment**, brings in relevant historical/scientific/artistic knowledge, and composes a reader's growing desire to understand or intervene. Its ghost reader can test transitions and comprehension, but not certify literary pleasure or critical value.

**Do not treat `final.md` as explanation layered over code or as a prose copy of the tutorial.** The two texts may initiate experiments independently. Simulations and observations may revise either, both or neither, with reasons and versioned evidence.

The missing intermediary is **a knowledge–critical-attention–composition process**:

`current artifact / observation / source → research pool → critical lenses → knowledge-desire selection → paragraph cards → competing routes → final.md → ghost reader and human review → text simulation / Godot experiment → observation → revised pool, texts and possibly task graph`.

This method extends `doc/book/RECURSIVE_ARCHITECTURE.md`, not a new book renderer or second canonical index.

## 1. Existing sources of truth and their limits

### Confirmed in the inspected repository

| `commons/maps/<Map>/final.md` | Canonical hall-level reflective writing | Do not overwrite until a reviewed revision is selected |
| `commons/maps/<Map>/tutorial.md` | Canonical hall-level reconstructable lesson | Keep tutorial review independent of final review |
| `commons/maps/<Map>/map_data.json` and artifact scripts | Authored spatial/operational source | Verify claims against actual revision and, as needed, runtime |
| `doc/tasks/_schema.md` and existing `doc/tasks/randomness_research*.json` | Task goals, dependencies, status, review and verification | Reconcile/augment, never regenerate completed or claimed work blindly |

### Recovered 13 October writing model (user-provided working account)

The earlier writing desk described a **research pool**, a graph-to-line problem, paragraph cards, A/B route trials, bounded readings of philosophical/rhetorical movement, and a ghost student. Its six original paragraph fields were **Information / Job / Attitude / Reader's gain / Bridge / Size**. Its Random Definition comparison used the same selected knowledge connections in two differently written routes, not rearranged identical paragraphs. A/B evaluation favoured the first route's consequence-led opening with the second route's historical braiding.

The account also distinguished **installed behaviour, historical evidence, editorial interpretation and unbuilt proposal**; a missing source was not to be glossed into a fluent transition. Do not infer that every feature of the described local writing desk is already in the checked-out Git branch. **Inventory existing Ada Writer / encyclopedia components before implementing a new interface.**

## 2. The core epistemological distinction: good information vs good knowledge *here*

A technical fact can be true, relevant to an artifact and still unnecessary in this paragraph. A historical reference can be accurate and arrive before the reader has a reason to want it. A theoretical association can be interesting but too detached from the operational object to make a defensible critical claim.

The admission test for the `final.md` pool is not only “is it correct?” but **“why does this knowledge belong at this exact moment, and what does it change for the reader?”**

Evaluate potential connections across four independent dimensions:

1. **Situated and supportable:** traceable to a source, observed operation, defined formula, identifiable geometry or explicitly labelled speculation.
2. **Desired:** follows an anomaly, attachment or unresolved question that gives the reader a reason to pursue it.
3. **Transformative:** changes a prior description, question, assumption, perceived relation or sense of the object's limits.
4. **Generative:** can lead to another observation, experiment, bodily action, reconstruction, historical comparison or question.

These are editorial tests, **not weights in a mandatory score**. A historically necessary paragraph may primarily supply context; a precise definition may simply let the reader make an otherwise impossible distinction. Some moments deserve to linger without proving their usefulness in the next line.

Keep a reserve of knowledge that is valuable but poorly placed. Do not force it into the draft or discard it permanently.

## 3. The four critical lenses: concrete operational meanings

### EDGE — the boundary of an operation

Question: *Where does this apparatus stop, clip, exclude, fail, threshold or refuse?*

Typical investigations: fixed cells, truncated precision, controller reach, permitted coordinate plane, selection eligibility, finite state, unwalkable slope, numeric tolerance, simulation boundary, runtime performance.

Required anchor: a particular rule, limit, parameter, scene behaviour or demonstrable counterexample. The limitation can be useful or protective, not inherently oppressive.

**Random Definition:** RGB values change; cell count and positions remain fixed. The edge is specific to this implementation, not proof that randomness lacks novelty.

### LEAK — what a record or representation does not keep

Question: *What goes missing between event, measurement, simulation, display, archive and interpretation?*

Typical investigations: a histogram omits adjacency; a seed alone omits draw order; a screenshot omits haptic timing; a trajectory sample omits continuous movement; a displayed line need not be a collider; a textual hypothesis does not establish a running result.

Required anchor: specify **which input**, **which transformation**, **which output**, and **which omitted property**. Do not call an information loss a mathematical error if the measured quantity was intentionally narrower.

**Random Entropy:** sorting preserves symbol counts and first-order Shannon entropy while changing neighbours. Preserve the variable, alphabet and formula when making this claim.

### TECHNICAL BIAS — the decisions that shape possible outcomes

Question: *Which choices of sampling, units, coordinates, distribution, threshold, renderer, classifier, controller or default favor one representation or action over another?*

Required anchor: the actual chosen mapping and a plausible alternative or tested intervention. **Distinguish technical/design bias from evidence of social or political bias.** Moving from one to the other requires an argued relation and, where claimed, affected users or evidence.

**Random Definition:** three successive draws are assigned to R/G/B. An alternative mapping can assign them to height. Both are decisions about what the result controls; the RNG itself does not prescribe either.

### ATTACHMENT — the reason an encounter matters to someone

Question: *What does a visitor want to preserve, wear, follow, enter, escape, repeat or refuse?*

Typical investigations: colour relations preferred over successful replay; a difficult route chosen over a smooth one; a sculpture that invites physical identification; a surprising glitch someone wants to keep.

Required anchor: either a design invitation (as a possibility), an identifiable artistic interpretation, or a reported human encounter. **Do not invent visitor feelings or declare AI-generated affective assessments to be observations.**

**Random Definition:** the prompt to keep a patch is an invitation. A visitor actually reporting attachment would require recorded evidence. The sleeve is a possible future use, not an installed effect.

### Relationship among the lenses

An attachment may identify an edge; the edge may expose a bias; the bias can suggest a new receiver; the new receiver may leak information the old one preserved. These movements should be traced in their actual order. **Do not demand a complete four-lens inventory in every chapter.** Some chapters will work through one lens; others will be driven by an anomaly outside this vocabulary.

## 4. Scientific, mathematical and artistic boundaries

For every critical claim, record at least its epistemic type:

- **SOURCE** — exact checked code, map, manuscript passage, measurement definition or documented historical claim. Source existence does not prove VR behaviour.
- **RUNTIME TEST** — actual executed test with build, steps, input state, results and limits.
- **CAPTURE** — screenshot/video and method, including what it cannot show.
- **HUMAN ENCOUNTER** — attributed/consented account of a person's interaction under described conditions.
- **INTERPRETATION** — a motivated critical or aesthetic reading that may coexist with alternatives.
- **HYPOTHESIS / TEXT SIMULATION** — conditional possible behaviour; not observed.
- **PROPOSAL** — a scene, interaction or text not yet implemented.

Do not merge probability with entropy, source unpredictability with visual irregularity, chaos with new random forcing, a displayed boundary with physical collision, or aesthetic pleasure with a measured variable. When discussing QFEP, preserve it as the project's proposed theoretical/artistic framework and distinguish Shannon entropy from variational free energy and physical thermodynamic entropy.

A useful critical association has two linked records: **the technically supported anchor** and **the interpretive move**. Either may be revised independently. An encounter can refute a proposed interpretation without invalidating the underlying formula.

## 5. Research pool schema and decision process

Start with a lightweight JSON pool per hall, referencing existing assets and experiment records. The example package includes `EXAMPLE_Random_Definition_knowledge_and_routes.json`.

Suggested item fields:

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `hall`, `anchor_artifact` | Stable identity and exact place of encounter |
| `claim` | One concrete, bounded proposition; avoid bundles of assertions |
| `knowledge_kind` | `operational`, `historical`, `mathematical`, `critical`, `artistic`, `speculative` |
| `epistemic_status` | `source_checked`, `runtime_checked`, `historically_sourced`, `interpretation`, `hypothesis`, `proposal`, `needs_research` |
| `evidence_refs` | Paths/URLs plus revision or snapshot; no invented runtime evidence |
| `critical_lenses` | Zero or more of `edge`, `leak`, `technical_bias`, `attachment`, each with a stated referent |
| `why_here` | The reader's currently live question or attachment |
| `transformative_relation` | Which earlier understanding this changes, if any |
| `experimental_affordance` | A bounded intervention or next observation; may be `null` |
| `links` | Related connection IDs, adjacency alternatives, history/theory associations |
| `disposition` | `selected`, `reserve`, `needs_research`, `deferred`, `rejected` with reason |

**Selection loop:** collect without flattening → verify basic grounding → write possible critical interpretations separately from verified mechanisms → identify the reader's current desire/question → shortlist only what changes that inquiry → preserve the unused pool → compose a reading route.

If an artifact sparks a compelling passage that exceeds the current installation, examine recovery or an artifact-development task before cutting it. This extends the repository's existing review hierarchy.

## 6. The paragraph card — eight functional questions

The 13 October method's six fields remain canonical. Add two as optional explicit prompts, not mandatory prose categories.

| Card | Writer's question | Example (Random Definition) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Information** | What precise knowledge enters? | The seed is unchanged; a draw is discarded before RGB assignment |
| **Job** | What must this paragraph do? | Undermine the expectation that a seed names an image |
| **Attitude** | From what stance does it speak? | Curious and exact, leaving room to prefer the changed picture |
| **Reader's gain** | What new distinction is available afterward? | Starting state is not the same as the complete procedure |
| **Critical pressure** | Which edge/leak/bias/attachment becomes newly visible? | The draw's meaning is supplied by RGB interpretation; the picture's geometry stays fixed |
| **Experimental potential** | Can the association become a test? | Keep 48 draws; map the triples to height instead of only colour |
| **Bridge** | Why does the next connection belong now? | The wish to return asks why random numbers became retrievable |
| **Size** | How much duration is justified? | Enough for a first-cube example; no restart of the Colour tutorial |

A paragraph need not have a critical pressure or a proposed build. Its `bridge` should be a particular reader's changed question or an intentional interruption, **not** generic “now some history.” The `size` is a provisional space allowance, not a formula for all halls. Record any source requirements and any previous encounter this paragraph transforms.

## 7. From a graph to a chapter: alternative reading routes

The research pool is a graph; the published passage is a time-based path. **Do not assume the best topological or semantic connection is the best narrative transition.**

Run a small A/B route trial with the **same selected knowledge connections** and comparable word allowance. The prose and bridges may be rewritten to fit each route: this tests competing editorial constructions, not identical paragraphs in different positions.

For Random Definition, compare:

- **Route A — consequence first.** Begin with +1 DRAW and the disagreement; uncover its procedure; visit RAND, the falling page, the sphere and the possibility of changed rules.
- **Route B — encounter/history braid.** Begin with the desire to recover a patch or with the sphere's bodily return; move between machine and historical promise before explaining the discarded draw.

Do not confuse this literary A/B with the existing **RGB versus RGB+height** implementation experiment. They need separate IDs, comparison methods and evidence.

For each route create a paragraph timeline, then test its transitions. Ask of every important return: **Does this new encounter make something earlier more interesting than it was before?** Keep productive friction, strange leaps and pauses where their consequences are felt. A perfectly smooth chain can become generic explanatory prose.

The 13 October consolidated preference was B's historical braiding with A's stronger visible-disagreement opening. That is a working editorial result, not proof that one fixed template should govern 200+ rooms.

## 8. Ghost reader, ghost student and human review — distinct jobs

### Technical ghost student (`tutorial.md`)

Input: previous checked learner project, current printed lesson, declared supplied infrastructure, exact expected output and test instructions.

Tasks: reconstruct from only the stated inheritance; flag missing references, code, methods, controls and prerequisites; predict one change; deliberately test one plausible failure; independently compare result with stated mechanism.

Output: construction trace, exact source/probe evidence, missing dependency and unresolved learner questions. **AI reconstruction is an automated teaching check, not evidence that an independent human learned.**

### Sequential ghost reader (`final.md`)

Input: one candidate draft, the active chapter context, a deliberately bounded previous-knowledge profile, and its paragraph timeline. Withhold later paragraphs.

For each paragraph: read only what is exposed so far. Report (a) what object or action is currently imaginable, (b) what mechanism is understood and what remains unknown, (c) what question/desire the paragraph creates, (d) what it changes about an earlier moment, (e) whether the next promised bridge feels motivated, forced or productively strange, and (f) any claim needing a source or behavior test.

After the final paragraph: report the strongest unanswered question, the point where desire or attention declined, the paragraph that prematurely told the reader the thesis, and any critical analogy that appears unearned. Compare the A/B routes using their reasons, not a numerical rating alone. An AI reader can flag coherence and plausible reader expectations; **it cannot certify lived pleasure, critical originality or real VR attachment**.

### Human artist/editor checkpoint

Review the material encounter, scientific grounding, literary rhythm, associative potential, source provenance and what remains worth investigating. Decide `retain`, `revise`, `develop_artifact`, `research_source`, `defer`, or `keep_open_question` with evidence/reason. Do not automatically select a route by ghost score. A negative or dull result is evidence worth retaining.

### Human visitor/learner later

Test reconstructability, intelligible encounter, actual reach/readability and whether observations or attachments occur. Record consent, order, prior knowledge, headset/build and limitations. Human findings may challenge both AI reading and author assumptions.

## 9. Integrate with text simulation and Godot, without confusing states

**Only selected passages should be converted to computational propositions**. A literary sentence is not a full specification, and a model's predicted outcome is not a Godot result.

For an admitted experiment:

1. Preserve the selected passage and its SHA/recoverable source version.
2. State the exact operational anchor and identify where literary interpretation begins.
3. Write one or several explicit interpretations, assumptions and exclusions.
4. Text-simulate possible states, including plausible failures. Mark as hypothetical.
5. Build one bounded Godot variant, preferably within the existing room; record scene/build identity.
6. Establish baseline → change one condition → observe → keep → replay → independently reconstruct → decide next change.
7. Review `tutorial.md` and `final.md` separately; either may be revised, retained with reason or left open.
8. Update the pool and, when evidence warrants it, the future task graph. Preserve the preceding version and decision.

The already specified `seed-bench-001` RGB/height experiment provides this first bounded implementation. **Do not invent a second independent persistence layer for the same values**, and do not replace its 4×4 reference with a new geometry without recording an explicit variant.

**Cross-hall transfer is a separate test level.** A record that reproduces inside one instrument does not prove portability into a different receiver. Headset comfort, spatial accessibility and human learning also require separate checks.

## 10. Worked editorial pilot: Random Definition

### Candidate pool (ordered provisionally, not all destined for prose)

1. `R01` Seed/draw mismatch: +1 DRAW changes RGB grouping under a stable seed. **SOURCE**: current `final.md`, tutorial, seed bench source; runtime scope must be checked against current build.
2. `R02` Desired colour neighbours: an invitation to keep a patch, **ATTACHMENT hypothesis**, not an observed visitor preference.
3. `R03` RAND 1955 table: historically produced fixed digits reusable by location. **HISTORICAL** source needed; verify details with RAND's production account before final publication.
4. `R04` Moving-number page: fixed table analogy frustrated by disappearing cells. **SOURCE** in `final.md`; verify actual timing and retention in its script/runtime if claims will be strengthened.
5. `R05` Returning sphere: bodily involvement, fixed return vs variable excursion. **HYPOTHESIS/SEPARATE ARTIFACT** until interaction is checked.
6. `R06` Shannon entropy omits adjacency because the specified meter counts symbol frequencies. **MATHEMATICAL + SOURCE**; compare equal histograms, altered order in `Random_Entropy`.
7. `R07` RGB as a choice of receiver: a draw has no native colour role. **OPERATIONAL/TECHNICAL BIAS**.
8. `R08` Height interpretation of same forty-eight draws. **PROPOSAL**, linked to `seed-bench-001`; not run.
9. `R09` A connected/wearable sleeve. **LITERARY PROPOSAL**; do not imply present force-bearing connections or cloth physics.

### Indicative eight-movement paragraph timeline

| Movement | Reader's question | Paragraph job | Pressure | Next bridge |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Visible discrepancy | Why did one image change? | Open with consequence | Attachment + operational anomaly | Investigate the unchanged number |
| 2. Procedure | Why didn't the seed preserve the image? | Explain generator/request roles | Technical bias | The promise of returning |
| 3. History | Why did people want reusable chance? | Give RAND a reason to enter | Historical complication | Return depends on retrieval |
| 4. Falling page | Can I reopen the lost line? | Make a promise fail materially | Leak | Other kinds of return |
| 5. Sphere | What is the same after a journey? | Move from representation to body | Edge / attachment | Compare permitted actions |
| 6. Colour and geometry | Who decided what could change? | Expose variable vs fixed properties | Technical bias / edge | Ask what else could be done |
| 7. Imagined sleeve or height study | What would a changed receiver make possible? | Open a buildable proposition without claiming it exists | Speculation | Need for a new experiment |
| 8. Hand-off to entropy | What does the next gauge preserve? | Revisit the patch through a new measure | Leak | Visit the next hall |

This is a **draft planning experiment**. The current canonical `Random_Definition/final.md` includes a textile panel description while the more recent illustrated editorial review describes relocating those panels to 10 PRINT. Confirm **current map, source, local uncommitted work and runtime** before writing as if the relocation is installed. Similarly, note that `R06` belongs primarily to the next hall, and do not exhaust that encounter in the previous chapter.

### The pilot's decisive editorial result

The pilot must demonstrate *why* a piece of knowledge was selected and *what changed because it entered*. It does not pass merely because the prose mentions all four critical lenses, or because the ghost reader gives it a high score. At least one strong bridge, one grounded critical inference, one preserved open possibility, and one evidence-linked choice to revise/retain/defer should be inspectable.

## 11. Proposed file integration (minimal, no live changes now)

Do not create an independent encyclopedia or migrate all chapters. Suggested proposal, subject to reconciliation with existing writing-desk components:

```text
doc/book/
    RECURSIVE_ARCHITECTURE.md             # existing; add a link upstream
    FINAL_KNOWLEDGE_COMPOSITION.md        # proposed method document
    critical-composition/                 # proposed planning companions
        README.md
        pools/Random_Definition.json
        routes/Random_Definition.A.json
        routes/Random_Definition.B.json
        reviews/Random_Definition.md
        templates/knowledge-connection.json
        templates/paragraph-card.json
```

Keep raw pool and draft prose independently versioned. Link knowledge connections to the existing experiment IDs, not copied observation logs. Use Git SHA or recoverable snapshot bytes and hashes. Preserve route variants, source decisions and unused branches. No canonical `final.md` mutation until editorial review.

Before implementing UI, **inspect existing writing-pattern and paragraph-route features in the local encyclopedia and Ada Writer**, including their current data stores and editing capabilities. The recovered 13 October account describes an interface but its complete current Git-backed implementation was not verified in this audit. Reuse working infrastructure if present.

## 12. Implementation work packages — proposed, not registered

A compatible draft goal is supplied as `PROPOSED_TASKS_final_critical_composition.json`; reconcile it with the existing `randomness_research_writing` W001–W005 tasks before adding any new tracker entries.

**Work order:**

1. **Inventory and reconcile** the 13 October writing pool/paragraph tools, `final.md` sources, existing research experiments, editorial plans and task files. Record what is already functional vs proposed.
2. **Define the pool contract** and the four critical lenses with source-scoped examples and a JSON validator. Start with one hall, not a museum-wide migration.
3. **Implement paragraph cards and route variants** using the original six fields plus critical pressure/experimental potential. Retain unused connections and previous versions.
4. **Run Random Definition A/B writing pilot** on the same selected pool items, with source checked claims and comparable length; preserve both drafts, their paragraph routes and the reasons for the editorial choice.
5. **Run ghost reader + source audit** with paragraph-reveal protocol. Output typed findings and human editorial decisions; do not treat scores as proof.
6. **Link one selected final proposition** to existing `seed-bench-001`. Use its text-sim / Godot/reconstruction experiment contract; do not run a fabricated test or promise a sleeve.
7. **Perform reciprocal review** after actual evidence: reconsider tutorial and final independently, identify learning debt, then allow the task plan to continue, redirect, defer or stop.
8. **Document and edition-proof** the approach: recoverable sources, decisions, open material, no silent mutation of frozen reading editions.

### Verification contract

- **Static knowledge integrity:** stable IDs, existing path/anchor references, explicit evidence states, no phantom scene, valid pool-to-paragraph links, retained reserve items, reproducible candidate route IDs.
- **Technical grounding:** exact formula/source where an operational claim requires it; code inspection separated from running tests.
- **Composition integrity:** both A/B routes use the same admitted knowledge items; paragraph jobs and bridges are inspectable; no forced four-lens checklist.
- **Ghost reader test:** sequential withheld-paragraph trace and transparent reported limitations.
- **Experiment integrity:** source snapshots, interpretations, text hypothesis, actual run and human-learner evidence correctly distinguished; no automatic claim that `seed-bench-001` has run.
- **Editorial result:** explicit retain/revise/develop/defer judgment and why; contradictory accounts remain available.
- **Integration:** generated companion records link to `RECURSIVE_ARCHITECTURE.md` and task plan without overwriting canonical hall texts or creating a competing book index.
- **Runtime/VR:** only necessary for actual scene edits; never inferred from passing a JSON validator or an AI-generated screenshot description.

Existing useful commands once local paths are available:

```bash
python -X utf8 doc/book/experiments/validate_experiments.py
python -X utf8 doc/book/course/randomness-research-2026-10-14/validate_plan.py
python tools/map_pathfinder.py check Random_Definition --verbose

git diff --check
```

The pathfinder applies if map placement changes; the first two commands validate existing contract/plan structure, **not literary quality or an actual headset run**. The proposed pool/route validator would need to be written and tested as part of implementation, not invoked as though already available.

## 13. Decisions to preserve and decisions still open

**Already established by user direction / prior collaboration:** tutorial and final are distinct reciprocal practices; the recursive text/world loop; the seven-step experiment verification; ghost student for reconstruction; the knowledge pool and six-field paragraph card; the importance of critical edges, leaks, technical biases and attachments; scientific/geometric grounding; associative strangeness; and the right of future observations to change writing and task order.

**Proposed here (not yet implemented or author-accepted as exact format):** an explicit editorial knowledge/critical-composition stage, two optional card fields, a concrete pool schema, the ghost-reader reveal protocol, its storage paths and this exact eight-task packaging. These are starting specifications for review and local implementation, not discoveries already tested.

**Still open:** whether the recovered writing workbench stores data in a format reusable by the book pipeline; how to expose pool/route decisions in the encyclopedia UI; what additional lenses arise from other halls; whether the ghost-reader test finds useful problems; whether readers experience the proposed associations; whether the first implementation generates a genuinely interesting revision; and which future experiment observations justify.

## 14. Agent handoff — first actual action

**First action is a read-only reconciliation**, not a rewrite or a new hall. Open the inspected repository paths and compare them with local uncommitted work and the 13 October writing desk. Produce a single-page inventory: existing tools and storage, missing contracts, conflicting text/artifact placements, best place for companion files, and which proposed tasks would duplicate W001–W005.

Then create only the minimal Random Definition knowledge pool and A/B paragraph cards in staging. Run the ghost-reader and source-check pass and return the two texts and a short evidence report for editorial review. No one should edit `commons/maps/Random_Definition/final.md` before that choice. If the passage requires behaviour that is missing, open an explicitly proposed artifact task and preserve the passage rather than silently deleting its possibility.

**Completion standard:** a reader can trace a paragraph from an operationally grounded claim through its critical pressure, the reason it enters the chapter, its place in a tested reading route, and—where selected—into a text simulation and a Godot experiment that may change the paragraph again.

# What chance is allowed to do

<!-- @random_touch -->

We stand before a small abacus. Five thin rods sit one above another, each a metre long, with a dark bead waiting at its centre. Behind them, a pale wall waits for marks.

We touch the first bead. The hand visible in the room follows it sideways. Our viewpoint stays still. The bead slows into one position, then departs for another. We can see how far it is allowed to go. Its next turn remains uncertain.

At the next row, the hand follows the same path twice as quickly. The third doubles that pace; the fourth doubles it again. The positions repeat. The rods have not grown, but there is less time inside the same distance. At the fifth bead, we return to the second row's pace. The visible hand rises and falls as well as moving sideways. The bead leaves the line that first seemed to contain it.

Small transparent circles gather behind the moving bead. Where they overlap, the wall darkens. We withdraw our hand. Its visible position follows our own movement again; the bead returns alone to its centre. The marks stay. Movement has left something we can examine without continuing to move.

The wall records twelve positions within each step. A faster bead draws sooner; after the same number of steps, the first four rows hold the same pattern. The fifth spreads its marks above and below the rod. The targets were selected uniformly, giving equal chances to equal intervals. The marks also include the journey between targets. A crowded middle can suggest a Gaussian distribution: a bell-shaped spread with most values near the average. Here, a central mark may record a crossing rather than a destination. The resemblance does not establish a Gaussian source.

The positions are kept in the program. We press REPLAY: the paper clears. We touch the first bead again. The turns return in the same order, and the marks gather again. The next movement can still be unfamiliar, even though the whole sequence has been kept.

<!-- @random_number_book_page_1955 -->

Further into the room, we come to a large page of falling numbers. A small stand in front says “select”. The numbers arrive from above, one row at a time, in groups of five digits. We touch a group. It turns amber and stays while the surrounding numbers continue downwards. We take our hand away. The digits remain.

Our touch has acquired another consequence. At the bead, we began a movement that left marks. Here, we keep a group already passing through the page. We have made a small still place in the fall.

RAND's *A Million Random Digits*, published in 1955, made a supply of numbers available for calculations using random selections. Producing that supply required testing and correction: its electronic source introduced biases, systematic departures from the intended even distribution. The published table preserved the results after further processing. Random numbers could be returned to at a numbered page. [RAND's production account](https://www.rand.org/pubs/monograph_reports/MR1418.html).

This falling page uses generated digits. The same sequence takes different forms: colour in the window, five digits on the page. We have selected a group that was already there. What we have changed is how long those digits stay in view. The rows move on around them. We read the five digits again.

<!-- @geiger_counter -->

The hall’s random-generating instruments share a beginning: 435. The colour window, the virtual lava lamps, the Geiger machine, even the falling page start from that number. Their differences are already visible. One beginning has become colours, rising forms, clicks and a path.

Click. A gap. Another click. The Geiger machine is already running. A physical Geiger counter detects radiation; this one calculates a sequence of detection times. No radioactive source is connected. We replay the sequence and hear the same gaps return.

435 is its seed: the number used to set the generator's starting state. Each calculation changes that state and supplies another value, which becomes a waiting time before a click. The seed stays 435 while the state advances. Resetting the same procedure to that beginning, with the same settings, produces the same sequence. This is pseudorandom generation: a repeatable calculation whose results can be difficult to anticipate.

The number has a history. A saved receipt records 435 arriving from RANDOM.ORG's atmospheric-noise service on 13 October 2026. The window reuses that receipt when the hall opens; it makes no fresh request on arrival. An acquired number has become a kept beginning. Its origin does not make every later click a new measurement of the atmosphere.[^arrival]

A seed need not be chosen randomly. At the colour window we can select a different number directly. It becomes the starting seed throughout the hall. RESET 435 restores the saved beginning; no new random selection is needed. The calculation remains; its beginning changes. Sharing 435 also does not make every object perform the same sequence: the generator, the order of requests and the assignment of values to colour, time or position matter too.

The visible hand's curve may appear random while following stored positions. The clicks may resist anticipation while repeating exactly. Our impression depends partly on what we can perceive and remember. Within a deterministic calculation, a fixed state and the same inputs supply no fresh uncertainty. The next encounter changes an input.[^entropy]

<!-- @seed_replay_demo/movement_sampler -->

A small dark sphere waits beneath six coloured traces. We pick it up, carry it and turn it. The traces show changes in position and rotation. After a sufficient recording, we release it and a seed appears, a whole number between zero and 999.

The recording keeps positions, turns and times. A fixed calculation condenses those measurements into the displayed number.[^gesture] The window changes; the Geiger begins another sequence of gaps. Keeping the recording lets us derive that seed again. The movement supplies a new input; the numbers that follow are still pseudorandom.

There are only a thousand possible seeds here. Two different gestures can become the same number. We have not yet kept such a pair. Their traces could remain different while the window, given the same seed and settings, repeats its colours.

The first spheres gave numbers a movement. Here movement gives a number back. What could that number be allowed to do next?

<!-- @random_return -->

The larger dark sphere is already travelling out from the centre and back. We hold it and travel with it. At the entrance, the bead moved the visible hand; here the floor passes beneath us.

Direction and distance can change between excursions. The centre stays where it was.

We release it. The sphere continues without us.

It returns to the centre.

<!-- @ -->

[^arrival]: The saved [opening receipt](../../../algorithms/randomness/seed_replay/opening_seed.json) records the value, provider, range and acquisition time. Each random-generating instrument in Random Definition starts a private stream from the shared hall seed. A manual choice, restored record or completed gesture recording can change it. The [435 revision](../../../doc/book/iterations/2026-10-15-seed-435-middle/README.md) records implementation and verification. The frame trace measures timing without reseeding the hall.

[^entropy]: Offline does not mean isolated from physical inputs: local hardware can supply entropy, as described in the [Linux hardware-RNG documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/hw_random.html). [NIST's entropy-source guidance](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/90/b/final) distinguishes entropy sources from deterministic generators. The claim here concerns fixed-state computation, not the impossibility of physical randomness in a computer.

[^gesture]: The sampler stores timed positions and orientations at finite precision. It hashes the stored measurements, using a fixed calculation to produce a compact code, then reduces that code to an integer from 0 to 999. The record retains the measurements as well as the derived seed; the seed alone does not reconstruct the gesture. Desktop mode samples the carried point; VR mode samples the tracked controller. The six traces show changes between accepted samples, not the complete motion. See the [tutorial](tutorial.md) for recording, replay and reconstruction.
